title: Jupiter: The Giant Planet That's Like a Whole Solar System
summary:
Imagine a planet so huge that more than 1,300 Earths could fit inside it. That's Jupiter! It's the biggest planet in our solar system, and it's a gas giant — a giant ball of mostly hydrogen and helium. There's no solid ground to stand on. If you tried to skydive into it, you'd sink deeper and deeper until the pressure and heat squished you. Not a good idea!

Jupiter is the fifth planet from the sun. A spaceship trip there from Earth takes about 13 months. If you weigh 100 pounds on Earth, you'd weigh 253 pounds on Jupiter because its gravity is much stronger.

Jupiter has nearly 70 moons. One moon, Ganymede, is bigger than the planet Mercury. Another moon, Io, has volcanoes that shoot yellow sulfur 300 miles high! And Europa, a frozen moon, might have a liquid ocean under its icy crust. Scientists think that ocean could hide life.

Jupiter also has a giant storm called the Great Red Spot. It's a hurricane that has raged for centuries — and it's so big that nearly three Earths could fit across it. Even though Jupiter is the largest planet, it has the shortest day: just 10 hours!
why_it_matters: Jupiter shows how wildly different planets can be, and learning about it now is like a preview of the space questions your generation may get to answer.

background_read: Jupiter is named after Jupiter, the king of the Roman gods — the same god the Greeks called Zeus.
Its Great Red Spot is a storm so wide that the whole Earth could fit inside it.
NASA (the U.S. space agency) has sent spacecraft such as Juno to fly past Jupiter and take close-up pictures of its clouds and moons.
Article_Structure: WHO: Jupiter, the biggest planet in our solar system, along with its nearly 70 moons.
WHAT: A giant gas planet with no solid ground, stronger gravity, a centuries-old storm called the Great Red Spot, and a very short 10-hour day.
WHERE: Fifth planet from the sun, about a 13-month spaceship trip from Earth.
WHY: Studying it shows how different a planet can be from Earth — and one icy moon, Europa, might even hide life in a hidden ocean.

perspectives.description: Jupiter is like a mini solar system, with dozens of moons — Ganymede, Io and Europa — so there is plenty left to explore.
Jupiter is extremely dangerous: there is no ground to land on, and the crushing pressure and heat would destroy anything that sank too deep.
Europa's icy crust may cover a liquid ocean, which could possibly hold life — but we would need better robots to go and check.
